Field surveys across northern Australian waters indicate that newborns exhibit a disc width range of 17 to 19 centimeters [Lb = 17 to 19 centimeters] during the peak pupping season, which coincides with elevated summer sea surface temperatures. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], the gestation period from copulation to parturition was observed to be approximately 460 days [ab = approximately 460 days], reflecting the protracted embryonic development common among urolophid and dasyatid rays. This relatively lengthy gestation, when compared to smaller-bodied stingrays, likely reflects the energetic demands of yolk-dependent embryogenesis in a species that reaches a substantial adult body size. The age at birth provides a critical baseline for understanding early-life survivorship and the timing of the transition to exogenous feeding in coastal nursery habitats.

Males of Maculabatis astra attain sexual maturity at a disc width of roughly 47 centimeters [Lp = roughly 47 centimeters], a size threshold that corresponds to the onset of gonadal maturation and clasper calcification. Interestingly, the total length at puberty for males is also reported at 47 centimeters [Lp = 47 centimeters], indicating that the disc width and total length are nearly equivalent at this developmental stage, a morphological characteristic not uncommon among benthic batoids. Puberty in this species marks a significant shift in energy allocation, where somatic growth rates begin to decelerate as resources are increasingly directed toward reproductive structures. Comparative data from congeneric species such as Maculabatis gerrardi suggest that the timing of maturity is closely linked to local productivity regimes, with individuals in more oligotrophic environments maturing later and at slightly larger sizes. The reproductive tract of mature males shows pronounced testicular recrudescence during the pre-monsoon period, and spermatogenesis is highly seasonal in the wild.

The reproductive output of female Black-spotted whiprays is modest but consistent with a K-selected life-history strategy typical of many elasmobranchs. Each gravid female typically carries one to three pups per litter [N_R_i = one to three pups per litter], with litter size showing no clear correlation with maternal body size within the sampled population. Furthermore, reproductive frequency is believed to be low, with females producing just one litter every two years [F_R_i = one litter every two years], a reproductive schedule that places considerable demographic pressure on adult survivorship. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of Australian coastal waters at 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], this translates to a maximum reproductive rate that is closely tied to seasonal temperature cycles and prey availability. The combination of small litter size and extended inter-birth intervals suggests that population recovery from overfishing could be exceptionally slow, warranting careful management of inshore trawl fisheries where this species is captured as bycatch.

Adult females are capable of reaching an ultimate disc width of 78.2 centimeters [Li = 78.2 centimeters], a size that positions Maculabatis astra among the medium-to-large dasyatids inhabiting the continental shelf. In contrast, the ultimate disc width for males is substantially smaller at 66 centimeters [Li = 66 centimeters], revealing a pronounced sexual dimorphism in maximum body size that is consistent with the reproductive demands placed on females for accommodating developing embryos. Corresponding to these size differences, the ultimate wet weight of adult females can reach 12,000 grams [Wwi = 12,000 grams], whereas males attain a much lower asymptotic mass of 8,200 grams [Wwi = 8,200 grams]. This disparity in body mass has implications for dietary partitioning between the sexes, as larger females are capable of consuming larger, harder-shelled prey such as portunid crabs and stomatopods. The morphological divergence between sexes becomes increasingly apparent after the onset of puberty, with female growth trajectories remaining elevated for a longer duration post-maturation.

Maximum recorded longevity in wild populations of the Black-spotted whipray is estimated at approximately 29 years [am = approximately 29 years], a lifespan that aligns with the broader pattern of extended life histories observed across the Dasyatidae at a temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. This value was derived from tag-recapture data collected in the Gulf of Carpentaria and corroborated by vertebral band counts, providing strong empirical support for a slow-life-history strategy. The same thermal regime that governs early development (27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]) also appears to influence somatic maintenance costs throughout adulthood, with metabolic rates at this temperature falling within the predicted range for a batoid of this body size. Longevity of this magnitude, combined with delayed maturity and low fecundity, renders the species particularly vulnerable to anthropogenic mortality. Conservation assessments for Maculabatis astra should therefore prioritize the preservation of adult females in the population, as they represent the demographic cornerstone for long-term population persistence in a variable coastal environment.
